work.title: Schizophrenia and the Book of Changes
work.first_publication: Niekas fanzine, 1965; reprinted in The Shifting Realities of Philip K. Dick (ed. Lawrence Sutin, 1995)

source.note: Full essay not independently located in this corpus; grounded via a substantial quotation preserved in Sutin's introductory framing.

reading.synopsis: Writing for the science fiction fanzine Niekas in 1965, Dick attempts to give the schizophrenic's fearful, isolated perceptual experience an analytical coherence that might extend beyond purely personal pathology into a genuine alternative viewpoint on human experience. His central argument, per the surviving quotation, is that what distinguishes schizophrenic existence is its relationship to time: 'The schizophrenic is having it all now, whether he wants it or not; the whole can of film has descended on him, whereas we watch it progress frame by frame. So for him, causality does not exist. Instead, the a-causal connective principle which [quantum physicist] Wolfgang Pauli called Synchronicity is operating in all situations.' He compares this state to being 'under LSD,' 'engulfed in an endless now,' and -- in a moment of unusually direct self-disclosure for a published essay -- describes himself as 'schizoid affective,' a 'pre-schizophrenic personality,' framing his own fear of impending mental illness as inseparable from the intellectual argument he is making about the nature of schizophrenic time-perception.

structure.form: essay combining analytical argument about schizophrenic time-perception with direct authorial self-diagnosis

motifs: Schizophrenic experience reframed as a distinct, internally coherent relationship to time rather than mere pathological confusion
Synchronicity (borrowed from Wolfgang Pauli/Carl Jung) as an alternative organizing principle to ordinary linear causality
Direct authorial self-diagnosis and vulnerability embedded within an ostensibly analytical, third-person argument
The I Ching ('the Book of Changes') implicitly offered as a divinatory system whose acausal logic parallels the schizophrenic's own relationship to time
reading.significance: This 1965 essay is an important early data point for Dick's recurring self-diagnosis as 'schizoid' or 'pre-schizophrenic,' a fear that runs through his private journals and essays for the rest of his career and that biographers connect directly to his lifelong preoccupation with the reliability of perceived reality. Its analytical move -- treating schizophrenic time-perception as a coherent alternative framework rather than simple malfunction, and linking it to Jungian/Pauli synchronicity and the I Ching's acausal divinatory logic -- previews the sympathetic, non-pathologizing treatment of altered mental states that recurs throughout Dick's fiction, from Eye in the Sky's subjective-reality layers to the visionary experiences woven into VALIS.
reading.closing_note: Dick's willingness to describe himself as 'pre-schizophrenic' within what is nominally a piece of cultural/scientific analysis exemplifies how thoroughly his private psychological fears and his public intellectual arguments were intertwined throughout his career.
